summary: Proposes four cryptographic suites for IPsec that are compatible with the US National Security Agency's Suite B specifications, similar to the two suites in RFC 4308. It obsoletes RFC 4869 and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: IPsec leaves many choices open: which cipher, which hash, which key exchange. Two peers have to pick the same ones or they will not talk. RFC 6379 packages the choices that match the NSA's Suite B into four named bundles, so a product can ask for one bundle by name instead of listing every option. Two of the bundles also encrypt the traffic; the other two only check that it has not been tampered with.

questions: what are the suite b gcm and gmac suites
what is a ipsec ui suite
subtitle: Four ready-made IPsec option bundles that line up with the NSA's Suite B algorithms.

tldr.problem: IPsec offers many cryptographic options, and two peers need to agree on a matching set. Users who want the algorithms of the US National Security Agency's Suite B need a simple named way to ask for them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four named user interface suites, Suite-B-GCM-128, Suite-B-GCM-256, Suite-B-GMAC-128 and Suite-B-GMAC-256. Each fixes the algorithm choices for ESP and for IKEv2.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 4869 and is now Historic. The suites are only collections of option values and do not change the IPsec protocols.

today: RFC 6379 is an Informational document with Historic status. It has not been obsoleted, but the suites it defines are no longer the ones in current use, and it is best read as a record of how the Suite B requirements were expressed for IPsec. It obsoletes RFC 4869, and the companion document that carries the authentication methods is RFC 6380.

sections.title: What a UI Suite Is
sections.content:
RFC 4308 proposes two optional cryptographic user interface suites for IPsec. The two suites, VPN-A and VPN-B, represent commonly used present-day corporate VPN security choices and anticipated future choices respectively. RFC 4869 proposed four new suites based on implementations of the United States National Security Agency's Suite B algorithms.

As with the VPN suites, the Suite B suites are simply collections of values for some options in IPsec. Using a UI suite does not change the IPsec protocols in any way. This document narrows the scope of the suites in RFC 4869 while keeping the original suite names, and it lists the changes it made.

The memo also sets a naming rule, because the names are what two peers use to agree. An implementation that uses these suites must use the names given here, should not use different names for the suites that are described, and must not use these names for suites that do not match these values. The memo says these requirements are necessary for interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: A UI suite is a shortcut for a list of options. It changes nothing about how IPsec works; it only saves both ends from having to spell out every cipher and hash. The names matter, because the two ends use them to check they have picked the same thing.

sections.title: The Four Suite B Suites
sections.content:
Each suite gives choices for ESP, described in RFC 4303, and for IKEv2, described in RFC 5996. The four are told apart by two things: the strength of the cryptographic algorithms, and whether ESP provides both confidentiality and integrity or integrity only. The names are built from the AES mode and the AES key length that ESP uses.

The two GCM suites, Suite-B-GCM-128 and Suite-B-GCM-256, give ESP both integrity protection and confidentiality, using AES-GCM with a 16-octet integrity check value. The memo says either of them should be used when ESP integrity protection and encryption are both needed. The two GMAC suites, Suite-B-GMAC-128 and Suite-B-GMAC-256, give ESP integrity protection only, using AES-GMAC, and provide no confidentiality at all. The memo says either of them should be used only when there is no need for ESP encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Two of the bundles encrypt as well as check the traffic. Two only check it. Within each pair, one uses 128-bit keys and the other 256-bit.

sections.title: ESP and IKEv2 Choices in Each Suite
sections.content:
Suite-B-GCM-128 uses ESP encryption of AES with 128-bit keys and a 16-octet integrity check value in GCM mode, with the separate ESP integrity field set to NULL. For IKEv2 it uses AES with 128-bit keys in CBC mode, the pseudo-random function HMAC-SHA-256, the integrity algorithm HMAC-SHA-256-128, and the 256-bit random ECP group for Diffie-Hellman. Suite-B-GCM-256 is the same with 256-bit keys and a 16-octet integrity check value, HMAC-SHA-384, HMAC-SHA-384-192, and the 384-bit random ECP group.

The GMAC suites differ in the ESP direction. Suite-B-GMAC-128 sets ESP encryption to NULL and ESP integrity to AES with 128-bit keys in GMAC mode, and its IKEv2 choices are the same as those of the GCM-128 suite: AES with 128-bit keys in CBC mode, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-256-128 and the 256-bit random ECP group. Suite-B-GMAC-256 sets ESP encryption to NULL and ESP integrity to AES with 256-bit keys in GMAC mode, with AES-256 CBC, HMAC-SHA-384, HMAC-SHA-384-192 and the 384-bit random ECP group on the IKEv2 side.
sections.plainLanguage: Each bundle fixes the cipher for the protected traffic, the algorithm that checks the key exchange, and the curve used to agree the key. The 128-bit bundles use AES-128, HMAC-SHA-256 and the P-256 group; the 256-bit bundles use AES-256, HMAC-SHA-384 and the P-384 group.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document inherits all of the security considerations of the IPsec and IKEv2 documents it points at.

It adds one warning. Some of the security options specified in these suites may be found in the future to have properties significantly weaker than those that were believed at the time the document was produced. In other words, the memo treats the choices it fixes as a snapshot of what was considered strong enough then, and says that a later reading of those algorithms may change that judgement.
sections.plainLanguage: The security reasoning is inherited from the IPsec and key exchange documents. The memo also warns that an algorithm judged strong when the suites were written may not be judged so later.

sections.title: The IANA Registry
sections.content:
IANA maintains a registry called Cryptographic Suites for IKEv1, IKEv2, and IPsec. The registry consists of a text string and the RFC number that lists the associated transforms. The four suites in this document have been listed with this document as the reference, and the entries will be updated on approval.

The updated values for the registry are Suite-B-GCM-128, Suite-B-GCM-256, Suite-B-GMAC-128 and Suite-B-GMAC-256, each defined in RFC 6379.
sections.plainLanguage: The four names are recorded in the IANA registry of cryptographic suites, so that a product can look up what a name means.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 4869
sections.content:
The memo lists three changes from the document it replaces. The definitions of the suites for IKEv1 were removed. The IKE authentication methods were removed from the suite definitions, and now appear in RFC 6380. The requirements on rekeying in IKEv2 were removed.

The effect of these changes is the narrowing the memo describes: the suites now cover IKEv2 and ESP only, the authentication methods live in their own document, and the rekeying requirements were dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier version of these suites covered the older key exchange protocol as well, and carried authentication and rekeying rules inside them. This version drops all three, leaving only the ESP and IKEv2 algorithm choices.

items.title: GCM suites
items.text: ESP provides both confidentiality and integrity, using AES-GCM with a 16-octet integrity check value.

items.title: GMAC suites
items.text: ESP provides integrity only, using AES-GMAC. There is no encryption.

items.title: 128-bit suites
items.text: AES with 128-bit keys, HMAC-SHA-256, and the 256-bit random ECP group.

items.title: 256-bit suites
items.text: AES with 256-bit keys, HMAC-SHA-384, and the 384-bit random ECP group.
